glowstick.title: How a glow stick glows with no battery 🧪 | Ep. 1
glowstick.desc:
Snap a glow stick and it lights up with no battery, no bulb and no wire. Inside the tube floats a thin glass vial of hydrogen peroxide. Bend it, the glass cracks, and the peroxide meets diphenyl oxalate. They build a very unstable molecule that falls apart into carbon dioxide and hands its energy to a dye, which gives it off as light. That's cold light: almost no heat. Warm it up and it glows brighter but quits sooner; cool it down and it lasts longer. 🎃

Sources: Wikipedia "Glow stick" and "Chemiluminescence"; Compound Interest "The Chemistry of Glow Sticks"; Temple University Chemistry Demos "Chemiluminescence" (2024).

faces.title: Why you see faces everywhere 👻 | Ep. 2
faces.desc:
Two dots and a line, and your brain yells: face! That's pareidolia. Your brain runs an always-on face detector: your eyes can start moving toward a face in about a tenth of a second, and a 2020 brain-scan study found face-like objects handled by the brain's face areas, before being sorted back into plain objects within about a quarter of a second. Monkeys do it too, and in one study babies still in the womb turned toward a face-shaped pattern of three dots. Scientists describe the detector as tuned to never miss, even at the cost of false alarms. So that ghost in the curtains? Your face detector, doing its job. Where's the strangest face you've ever spotted?

Sources: Wardle et al., Nature Communications (2020); Crouzet, Kirchner & Thorpe, Journal of Vision (2010); Taubert et al., Current Biology (2017); Reid et al., Current Biology (2017); University of Sydney (Alais et al., 2021).

darkeyes.title: Why the dark gets less dark after 20 minutes 🌙 | Ep. 3
darkeyes.desc:
Turn off the lights and at first you see nothing. Wait twenty minutes and the room slowly appears. 🌙 Your rods rebuild a light-catching pigment called rhodopsin, and you can end up as much as a million times more sensitive. One bright flash undoes it, which is why pilots and ship crews use red light. Could you sit in the dark for twenty minutes?

Sources: Webvision (Univ. of Utah, NCBI Bookshelf) "Light and Dark Adaptation"; Univ. of Minnesota "Sensation and Perception"; Wikipedia "Adaptation (eye)" and "Rod cell".

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#halloween #howitworks #science #nightvision #Shorts

foxfire.title: Why some mushrooms glow in the dark 🍄 | Ep. 4
foxfire.desc:
Some mushrooms glow in the dark, with no battery and no fire. People call it foxfire: Aristotle wrote about its cold light, and it even lit the compass of the Turtle submarine in the 1770s. Inside the fungus, a fuel called luciferin reacts with oxygen, helped by an enzyme, and the energy comes out as green light. But why spend energy on light? A 2015 study in Brazil set out fake glowing mushrooms, and they drew far more insects than dark ones. Those insects may carry the spores to new wood. 🍄✨

Sources: Oliveira et al., Current Biology (2015); Kaskova et al., Science Advances (2017); Dartmouth Geisel School of Medicine; Wikipedia ("Foxfire", "Turtle (submersible)").

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#halloween #mushrooms #bioluminescence #science #Shorts

ouija.title: Who really moves the Ouija pointer? 👻 | Ep. 5
ouija.desc:
Rest your fingers on a Ouija pointer and it starts to move, but nobody means to push it. In 1853 Michael Faraday tested the same mystery with séance tables: he slipped a simple pointer between the sitters' hands and the table, and it showed their own hands were pushing, ever so slightly. Once they could watch it, the table stopped turning. It's the ideomotor effect: your brain expects a movement and your muscles make it, too small to notice. No ghosts needed. 👻

Sources: Faraday, letter to The Times (June 1853); Wikipedia "Ouija" and "Ideomotor phenomenon"; The Skeptic's Dictionary "ideomotor effect"; Gauchou, Rensink & Fels, Consciousness and Cognition (2012).

zombieant.title: The fungus that turns ants into zombies 🐜 | Ep. 6
zombieant.desc:
A real Halloween story: in tropical rainforests, the fungus Ophiocordyceps takes over carpenter ants. An infected ant leaves its nest high in the trees, wanders in a "drunken walk", then around noon bites the vein under a leaf about 25 cm above the ground, in humid air the fungus likes. Its jaw muscles waste away, so it stays put. Surprise: in 2017 scientists found the fungus wrapped around the ant's muscles, not in its brain. Days later a stalk grows from the back of its head and releases spores to infect more ants. Fossil leaves show the same bite marks 48 million years ago. And no, it can't infect you. Which nature fact creeps you out the most?

Sources: Hughes et al., BMC Ecology (2011); Fredericksen et al., PNAS (2017); Hughes, Wappler & Labandeira, Biology Letters (2010); NPR (2023).

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#halloween #zombieant #fungi #nature #Shorts

catseyes.title: Why cat eyes glow in the dark 🐈‍⬛ | Ep. 7
catseyes.desc:
In flash photos, a cat's eyes glow, but yours turn red. Why? Behind a cat's retina is a mirror-like layer called the tapetum lucidum. Light that slips past the light-sensing cells bounces back for a second chance, which helps cats make the most of dim light (with a little blur as the price). A phone flash sits right beside the lens, so that bounced light comes straight back into the camera. People have no mirror, so the flash lights up the blood-rich layer at the back of the eye instead: red-eye. 🐈‍⬛👀

Sources: Wikipedia ("Tapetum lucidum"); Colorado State University (Dr. Cynthia Powell, veterinary ophthalmologist); Mental Floss ("Why do we get red eye in photos?").

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#halloween #cats #catsofinstagram #science #Shorts

owl.title: How owls fly almost silently 🦉 | Ep. 8
owl.desc:
An owl can swoop right past you and you won't hear it. 🦉 Its wings have three tricks: a comb-like front edge, a soft fringed back edge that breaks up the turbulence, and a velvety surface that soaks up sound. Together they let the owl hear its prey without the prey hearing it coming. What would you make quieter with owl feathers?

Sources: Wikipedia "Owl"; University of Cambridge, "The owl and the wind turbine".

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#halloween #owls #howitworks #science #Shorts

spidersilk.title: Is spider silk stronger than steel? 🕸️ | Ep. 9
spidersilk.desc:
One thread of spider silk can stop a flying insect, but it isn't stronger than steel. Thread for thread, good silk is about as strong as a mid-range steel; it's about six times lighter, so for its weight, silk wins. It starts as a liquid protein in the spider's glands and hardens into a fibre as it's pulled out through the spinnerets, and an orb weaver can make up to seven kinds. The real trick is the catch: the stiff spokes absorb most of the impact, much of the energy turns into heat so the bug doesn't bounce out, and the stretchy sticky spiral holds it. Walk into a web this Halloween and you'll know why it clings. Did you think silk was stronger than steel?

Sources: University of Cambridge / The Conversation, "Spider silk is a wonder of nature, but it's not stronger than steel"; Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Is spider silk stronger than steel?"; Sensenig et al., J. R. Soc. Interface (2012); Babb et al., Nature Genetics (2017).

harvestmoon.title: Why the October moon looks huge and orange 🌕 | Ep. 10
harvestmoon.desc:
The October moon can rise huge and orange over the hills, but it isn't really bigger and it isn't really orange. Near the horizon, moonlight crosses much more air, which scatters the blue away (the same reason sunsets look red). And the size? Your fingernail at arm's length covers it low or high, and photos show the same width: the giant moon is an illusion in your brain. Even astronauts in orbit see it, and scientists still can't fully explain why. 🌕🍂

Sources: NASA Science ("The Moon Illusion"); NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day; StarDate (McDonald Observatory); Old Farmer's Almanac.

#halloween #moon #huntersmoon #astronomy #Shorts

pumpkin.title: Why a carved pumpkin rots so fast 🎃 | Ep. 11
pumpkin.desc:
Carve a pumpkin and in a few days its face starts to sag. An uncut pumpkin has a hard, waxy rind that keeps water in and germs out, and a pumpkin is about 90% water. Carving cuts right through that seal: water escapes, the flesh dries and softens, and airborne mould spores like Penicillium and Aspergillus move in with bacteria. A real candle's heat makes it worse. To slow it down, scoop out all the insides, keep it cool and out of the sun, put petroleum jelly on the cuts and use an LED light. 🎃

Sources: Utah State University Extension (2020); K-State Research and Extension (2024); Mississippi State University Extension; University of Illinois Extension.

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#halloween #pumpkin #jackolantern #science #Shorts

skeleton.title: Your skeleton is alive 💀 | Ep. 12
skeleton.desc:
Your skeleton isn't spooky, it's alive and busy right now. You were born with around 300 bones that fuse into 206. They hold you up, guard your brain, heart and lungs, and let your muscles move you. Inside some bones, soft marrow is a factory for red cells, white cells and platelets. Your bones are a calcium bank, and their cells keep tearing down old bone and building new: about 10% of an adult skeleton every year. 💀🎃

Sources: Cleveland Clinic "Skeletal System"; MedlinePlus "Bone Marrow Diseases"; Healthline "How Many Bones Does a Baby Have?"; Wikipedia "Bone" and "Bone remodeling".

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.

lock.title: How a Pin Tumbler Lock Really Works 🔐 | Ep. 13
lock.desc:
Your key is a tiny code. Here is how a pin tumbler lock actually reads it 🔑 Five little pins, one shear line, and a key that lines them all up.

Sources: Britannica "Lock" and "Linus Yale, Jr."; HowStuffWorks "How Locks Work"; Wikipedia "Pin tumbler lock".

match.title: How a Match Really Lights 🔥 | Ep. 14
match.desc:
Strike a match and fire appears, but much of the chemistry isn't on the match, it's on the box 🔥 The head holds the fuel (sulfur, antimony sulfide) and the oxygen supply (potassium chlorate). The striking strip holds red phosphorus: friction heats a trace of it, it ignites, and that sets off the head. Which everyday thing should we explain next? 👇

Sources: University of Washington Chemistry demo, Royal Society of Chemistry, Britannica, Compound Interest, AIChE CCPS.

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.

ship.title: How a Giant Steel Ship Floats 🚢 | Ep. 15
ship.desc:
A steel ship weighs thousands of tons, so why doesn't it sink? Because it pushes aside its own weight in water. Clay lump vs clay boat, Archimedes' principle, average density, and the Plimsoll line, in under 90 seconds.

Sources: NASA Glenn Research Center (Buoyancy); Britannica (Archimedes' principle, Plimsoll line); OpenStax University Physics; USGS Water Science School; IMO International Convention on Load Lines; Gard.

eclipse.title: How Solar and Lunar Eclipses Really Work 🌑 | Ep. 16
eclipse.desc:
The Moon can hide the Sun in the middle of the day 🌑 In a solar eclipse the Moon slides between us and the Sun; its shadow has a dark inner umbra (totality) and a fainter outer penumbra. In a lunar eclipse Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, which glows dim red. Why not every month? The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5°. Safety: solar eclipses need real eclipse glasses, not sunglasses.

Sources: NASA Science, Scientific American, Earth View Inc. eclipse viewing guide.

skyblue.title: Why the Sky Is Really Blue 🌤️ | Ep. 17
skyblue.desc:
Why is the sky blue, a sunset red and a cloud white? It is all light scattering: tiny air molecules scatter short blue waves far more than long red ones, sunset light crosses more air so the blue is scattered out, and big cloud droplets scatter every color about equally. Here is how it really works.

Sources: Met Office, UCAR SciEd, Royal Museums Greenwich.

magnet.title: Cut a Magnet in Half and You Get Two Magnets 🧲 | Ep. 18
magnet.desc:
Cut a magnet in half and you never get a "north piece". You get two magnets, every time. Inside iron, the electrons act like teeny magnets, and they line up in zones called domains. A nearby magnet swings those domains into line, which is why a nail sticks. Heat iron past about 770 °C and the order falls apart. Fridge magnets hide stripes of alternating poles, so they only grip on one side. So could anything ever have just one pole?

Sources: National MagLab "Magnetic Domains"; HyperPhysics (Georgia State) "Ferromagnetism"; Univ. of Illinois Physics Van; K&J Magnetics "Halbach Arrays"; CERN MoEDAL.

barcode.title: A Barcode Doesn't Hold the Price 🛒 | Ep. 19
barcode.desc:
A barcode doesn't hold the price or the name. All it holds is a number, and the store's computer looks up the rest. A scanner reads black bars (they soak up light) and white gaps (they bounce it back) as a signal, decodes seven-slice digits, and checks the last digit with a bit of math. The first item ever scanned was a pack of Juicy Fruit gum, in Troy, Ohio, on June 26, 1974.

Sources: GS1 (what a barcode encodes); Wikipedia "Universal Product Code" (structure, check digit, first scan, citing the Smithsonian and Wired); Scanbot and Triton (how laser scanners read bars).

search.title: Google Doesn't Search the Web When You Search 🔎 | Ep. 20
search.desc:
When you hit search, Google doesn't go out and search the web. It already did that. Crawlers follow links all day, and everything they find goes into an index of hundreds of billions of pages. Google compares it to the index at the back of a book. Your words pull up lists of pages, and the pages that match get ranked by meaning, relevance, quality, usability and context, all in a fraction of a second. What's the strangest thing you've ever searched?

Sources: Google "How Search works" (organizing information; ranking results); Google blog "Understanding searches better than ever before" (2019); Manning et al., Introduction to Information Retrieval.

faceid.title: Face ID Doesn't Look at Your Face 📱 | Ep. 21
faceid.desc:
Your phone doesn't look at your face. It looks at its shape. Face ID projects thousands of invisible infrared dots, reads where they land to build a depth map, and turns that into numbers that stay on your device. A printed photo has no depth, so it can't fool it.

Sources: Apple Support (About Face ID advanced technology); Apple Platform Security guide (Face ID and Touch ID security).

airfryer.title: Your Air Fryer Has Never Fried Anything 🍟 | Ep. 22
airfryer.desc:
Your air fryer has never fried anything. 🍟 It's a tiny countertop convection oven: a heater, a fan, and air whipping around at up to 200 °C. Fast air strips away the thin "blanket" of still air around your food, the outside dries, and the Maillard reaction turns it golden. So: fryer, or very small oven?

Sources: Wikipedia "Air fryer", "Convection oven" (boundary layer), "Maillard reaction"; Philips Airfryer launch 2010, inventor Fred van der Weij (via Wikipedia).

orbit.title: Orbit Is Falling and Missing the Ground 🛰️ | Ep. 23
orbit.desc:
To reach orbit, a rocket doesn't just go up. It goes sideways. The space station moves at about 17,500 miles per hour, fast enough that as it falls toward Earth, the ground curves away beneath it. Orbit isn't escaping gravity: at the station's height, gravity is still about 90 percent as strong. It's falling and missing the ground, which is why astronauts float.

Sources: NASA (What Is Microgravity?; Space Station Facts and Figures; Basics of Space Flight, Gravity & Mechanics; Technical Memorandum TM X-52396); NOAA SciJinks.

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#orbit #space #physics #howthingswork #Shorts

recommend.title: Only a Few Dozen Videos Ever Reach Your Screen 📱 | Ep. 24
recommend.desc:
Out of millions of videos, only a few dozen ever reach your screen. YouTube's engineers described it as a funnel: pull out a few hundred that viewers like you enjoyed, then score each one. Back in 2011 YouTube learned that a click doesn't mean you watched, so its 2016 system predicted watch time instead, and today surveys, shares, likes and dislikes count too. Instagram says its key Reels guesses are whether you'll watch to the end, like it or reshare it. So what does your feed think you are?

Sources: Covington, Adams & Sargin, "Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations" (2016); YouTube Official Blog, "On YouTube's recommendation system" (2021); Instagram, "Instagram Ranking Explained" (2023).

tap.title: How Tap-to-Pay Works With No Battery 💳 | Ep. 25
tap.desc:
A contactless card has no battery. So how does it pay when you tap? The terminal's coil makes a magnetic field that flips about 13.5 million times a second, and it powers the card's chip through a tiny wireless "transformer". Every payment uses a one-time code, so a recorded signal can't be replayed.

Sources: Wikipedia "Near-field communication" and "Contactless payment"; Apple Pay security overview; EMVCo.

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#tapandpay #nfc #howthingswork #technology #Shorts

flush.title: Your Toilet Doesn't Push, It Sucks 🚽 | Ep. 26
flush.desc:
Your toilet doesn't push the water down. It sucks it. 🚽 In most North American toilets, the bowl fills the curved trapway so fast that the whole pipe turns into a siphon, and that gurgle at the end is air breaking it. Puller or pusher: which one is yours?

Sources: Wikipedia "Flush toilet" and "Low-flush toilet"; US EPA WaterSense (Energy Policy Act 1992, 1.6 gpf); Explain That Stuff "How toilets work"; plumbing guides on bucket flushing (Benjamin Franklin Plumbing, HomeServe); Architizer "How to Specify: Toilets".

window.title: The Tiny Hole in Every Plane Window ✈️ | Ep. 27
window.desc:
That tiny hole at the bottom of a plane window isn't a flaw. Windows have three panes. The hole in the middle one lets cabin air into the gap, so the pressure pushing out lands on the outer pane, with the middle pane as a backup. It also lets moisture out so the window doesn't fog up.

Sources: ScienceAlert; Time (quoting Slate's Mark Vanhoenacker and GKN Aerospace's Marlowe Moncur); AirHelp.

#airplane #aviation #engineering #howthingswork #Shorts

hurricanewc.title: How a Hurricane Really Forms 🌀 | Ep. 28
hurricanewc.desc:
A hurricane is a giant heat engine, and its fuel is warm ocean water. The sea surface needs to be at least about 27 °C (80 °F). Warm, moist air rises, cools and condenses into storm clouds, releasing the heat that powers the storm. Earth's rotation turns the inflow into a spin: counterclockwise north of the equator, clockwise south of it. When sustained winds reach 74 mph it is officially a hurricane, with a calm eye inside an eyewall of the strongest winds. Which part surprised you most?

Sources: NOAA "Hurricanes"; NOAA JetStream "Tropical Cyclone Introduction" and "Tropical Cyclone Structure"; NHC Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale.

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#hurricane #weather #howthingswork #science #Shorts

submarine.title: To Dive, a Submarine Lets the Ocean In 🌊 | Ep. 29
submarine.desc:
To dive, a submarine lets the ocean in, on purpose. 🌊 So how does it ever come back up? Vents open, air rushes out, seawater floods the ballast tanks and it slips under. Trim tanks make it hover, diving planes steer, and a blast of compressed air pushes the water back out to bring it home. Would you trust a bubble of air to bring you home?

Sources: Wikipedia "Submarine", "Ballast tank", "Archimedes' principle", "Swim bladder", "Virginia-class submarine".

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#howitworks #science #submarine #physics #Shorts

wifi.title: How WiFi Gets Through Your Walls 📶 | Ep. 30
wifi.desc:
Your WiFi goes through walls. How? It isn't pushing anything solid. It's radio waves, about 12 cm from peak to peak, and a wall is barely in their way. Each wall just takes a small share, and metal, stone and water take the most. The 5 GHz band is faster but reaches less far.

Sources: Wikipedia "Wi-Fi" and "Microwave oven"; basic physics (c = f x wavelength).

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#wifi #howthingswork #explained #technology #Shorts

onion.title: Why Onions Really Make You Cry 🧅 | Ep. 31
onion.desc:
Why do onions make you cry? The onion isn't sad, it's defending itself. Cutting rips its cells open, so enzymes meet sulfur chemicals and make a stinging gas, syn-propanethial-S-oxide. The gas drifts into your eyes, your nerves warn your brain, and your tear glands flush it away.

Sources: Wikipedia "Lachrymatory factor"; Discover Magazine; The Conversation; Imai et al., Nature 2002.

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#onion #chemistry #howthingswork #science #Shorts

sleep.title: What Your Brain Does All Night 😴 | Ep. 32
sleep.desc:
When you sleep, your brain doesn't switch off. It runs through cycles of about 80 to 100 minutes, four to six times a night: deep slow-wave sleep early on, more REM later, when your eyes dart, your brain is about as active as when you're awake, and dreaming usually happens. Sleep helps form long-term memories, and in mice, researchers found the brain clears waste faster while asleep.

Sources: NHLBI/NIH (Stages of Sleep; Why Is Sleep Important?); Xie et al., Science 2013 (mouse study); Discover Magazine (why we dream is still debated).

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#sleep #dreams #brain #science #Shorts

snowwhite.title: Why Snow Is White When Ice Is Clear ❄️ | Ep. 33
snowwhite.desc:
Why is snow white if ice is clear? There's no white in snow at all. A snowbank is mostly air, packed with tiny clear ice crystals. Light bounces off and bends through crystal after crystal, and since ice barely absorbs visible light, every colour comes back out together: white. A smashed windowpane does the same thing. But poke a deep hole in fresh snow and it glows blue, because deep snow soaks up a little more red light. ❄️

Sources: NSIDC (National Snow and Ice Data Center), "Science of snow"; UCAR Center for Science Education; Live Science (Kenneth Libbrecht, Caltech).

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#snow #winter #science #physics #Shorts

yawn.title: Why Yawns Are Contagious 🥱 | Ep. 34
yawn.desc:
Why are yawns contagious? Scientists still argue. Just thinking about yawning can set one off. Dogs can catch human yawns (21 of 29 in one study, though later results were mixed), and some chimps yawn at videos of yawning chimps. Idea 1: brain cooling. With a cold pack on the forehead, people caught far fewer yawns (9% vs 41%). Idea 2: it's social, since yawns spread most among family. But the empathy link is contested: in 328 people, catching yawns tracked age, not empathy. 🥱

Sources: Gallup & Gallup, Evolutionary Psychology (2007); Gallup & Eldakar, Frontiers in Neuroscience (2013); Norscia & Palagi, PLoS ONE (2011); Bartholomew & Cirulli, PLoS ONE (2014); Joly-Mascheroni et al., Biology Letters (2008); Anderson et al. (2004); Provine, American Scientist (2005).

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#yawning #brain #psychology #science #Shorts

wrinklyfingers.title: Why Your Fingers Wrinkle in Water 🖐️ | Ep. 35
wrinklyfingers.desc:
Why do your fingers wrinkle in water? It's not just soggy skin: your nerves do it. Doctors noticed in the 1930s that fingers with a damaged median nerve stay smooth in water. In a warm soak, nerves make the tiny blood vessels under your fingertips narrow, the volume drops, and the skin on top is pulled into folds, only on hairless skin like fingertips, palms and soles. A 2025 study even found the same fingers wrinkle in the same pattern every time. Why? The leading idea is grip, but the studies disagree. Did you think it was just soggy skin?

Sources: Haseleu et al., PLoS ONE (2014); Wilder-Smith & Chow, Muscle & Nerve (2003); Kareklas, Nettle & Smulders, Biology Letters (2013); Binghamton University (2025).

handwarmer.title: How Hand Warmers Get Hot With No Battery 🔥 | Ep. 36
handwarmer.desc:
How do hand warmers get hot with no battery? The recipe is on the maker's own safety sheet: more than half iron powder, plus water, a pinch of salt, activated charcoal and vermiculite. Tear the pack open, air gets in through the cloth, and the iron starts to rust. Rusting always gives off heat; fine powder and salt just make it fast enough to feel, for hours. The clicky reusable kind is different: a liquid holding more dissolved salt than it normally could, which crystallises and releases stored heat when you click it. 🔥🧤

Sources: Kobayashi Healthcare safety data sheet (air-activated heating packs); University of Silesia (Prof. Robert Musioł); Minnesota State University, Mankato (Dr. Marie Pomije, via KTTC); BBC Science Focus.

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#handwarmers #winter #chemistry #science #Shorts

thermos.title: How a Thermos Keeps Drinks Hot and Cold ☕ | Ep. 37
thermos.desc:
How does a thermos keep drinks hot and cold? It has no idea which one it's holding. It doesn't make heat or cold; it just stops heat crossing, both ways. Heat travels by conduction, convection and radiation. The gap between a thermos's two walls is a near-vacuum, so heat can't conduct across and no air currents can carry it, and the silvered walls bounce infrared back. The weak point is the top, where the walls join, which is why the neck is narrow and the stopper is thick. James Dewar showed the idea in London on Christmas Day 1892, to keep liquid gases cold, and never patented it. Coffee or ice water in yours?

Sources: University of Sydney School of Physics (Thermos Flask); Royal Institution (Dewar flask, 1892); Encyclopaedia Britannica (vacuum bottle).

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#science #physics #howitworks #thermos #Shorts

popcorn.title: Why Popcorn Pops 🍿 | Ep. 38
popcorn.desc:
Why does popcorn pop? Each kernel holds a little water (about 13-14.5%) inside a tough hull. Heat it and the water gets hotter than boiling, the starch turns to gel, and at about 180 °C the pressure reaches around ten times normal air pressure. The hull cracks, the steam bursts out and the gel puffs into foam that sets solid in hundredths of a second. The pop sound? High-speed video shows it lines up with the steam rushing out, not the crack. 🍿

Sources: Virot & Ponomarenko, J. R. Soc. Interface (2015); Hoseney et al., Journal of Cereal Science (1983); Purdue University Agriculture (Hamaker, 2020).

🔔 Subscribe for a new explainer every day.
#popcorn #science #foodscience #physics #Shorts

coldbreath.title: Why You Can See Your Breath When It's Cold ☁️ | Ep. 39
coldbreath.desc:
Why can you see your breath when it's cold? Your breath is always full of water, as invisible water vapor. Warm air can hold lots of it, but air at freezing holds only about a tenth as much as air as warm as your body. So when your warm, wet breath hits the cold, it cools past its dew point, and the vapor sticks together into tiny droplets of liquid water: a little cloud. Real clouds form the same way, just way bigger. A second later it mixes with more dry air, and the droplets evaporate again. ☁️❄️

Sources: University of Washington, Dept. of Atmospheric Sciences; NOAA National Weather Service (dew point, JetStream "How clouds form"); Library of Congress, Everyday Mysteries.

staticshock.title: Why You Get More Static Shocks in Winter ⚡ | Ep. 40
staticshock.desc:
Why do you get more static shocks in winter? Every time your socks or shoes rub the carpet, tiny electrons hop from one material to the other, and your body piles up charge, up to thousands of volts (but only a tiny amount of charge, so it's just a sting). On humid days, a thin film of water on surfaces quietly drains that charge away. Cold winter air holds very little water, and heating it indoors doesn't add any, so the charge has nowhere to go... until you touch the doorknob. ⚡🚪

Sources: University of Kentucky Dept. of Physics & Astronomy; University of Wisconsin-Madison Physics ("Wonders of Physics"); University of Alaska Fairbanks Geophysical Institute (Alaska Science Forum); Northeastern University.
